shifts-movements-s1.title: A coffee shop's busy month
shifts-movements-s1.html: A coffee shop graphs the price of its iced latte against the number sold each day, with one downward curve labeled D for its customers' demand. Over one month: in week 1 the shop cuts the price of a latte from $5 to $4. In week 2 a large office building opens next door. In week 3 a rival cafe across the street starts giving away free iced tea.

items.q: Label this graph of a market. Price goes up the side, quantity goes across the bottom, and each curve carries its name.
The marked point is where the market starts. Place point X on curve S so that it shows a larger quantity and a higher price than the marked point.
On a graph with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis, which ordered pair plots the row for a price of $10?
What kind of relationship does the table show between the price of a ticket and the number of tickets sold?
options: An inverse relationship: as price rises, tickets sold fall
A direct relationship: as the price rises, tickets sold rise
No relationship: tickets sold do not depend on price
A relationship that rises and then falls

items.q: Using the table, by how many tickets a day do sales fall when the price rises from $8 to $12?

mistakes.why: That is the change in price ($12 - $8). The question asks for the change in tickets, the other column.
You added the two quantities. A change is the new value minus the old one: 400 - 200.

items.q: If the pattern in the table continues, how many tickets a day would the theater sell at a price of $14?
As the outdoor temperature rises over a week, a cafe sells fewer cups of hot chocolate. Which statement describes these two variables?
options: They have a direct relationship, moving together
They have no relationship
They have an inverse relationship
Temperature depends on cups sold

items.q: Which pair of variables is most likely to have a direct relationship?
options: The price of a snack and the number of snacks bought
Hours worked in a week and that week's pay
Hours spent on a phone game and hours left for sleep
The price of a bus fare and the number of riders

items.q: On a graph with hours studied across the bottom and test score up the side, point Q is (0, 40). What does it show?
options: A student who studied 0 hours and scored 40
A student who studied 40 hours and scored 0
A score that rose by 40 points
The average of 0 and 40

items.q: A reader checks your graph for its labeling point. Which features must it have? Select all that apply.
options: A label on the horizontal axis
A label on each curve
A title written above the graph
Each curve drawn in a different color

items.q: A student draws a market graph with Quantity up the side and Price across the bottom, and labels everything else correctly. What happens to the labeling point?
options: It is earned, because both axes carry a label
It is earned if the curves are drawn neatly
It is lost only if the curves are unlabeled too
It is lost, because the axes are swapped from the standard graph

items.q: A straight line passes through the points (2, 8) and (6, 4). What is its slope?

mistakes.why: You dropped the sign. The vertical value falls from 8 to 4 while the horizontal value rises, so the slope is negative.

items.q: As the price of a scooter rises from $4 to $10 (hundreds of dollars), the number sellers offer rises from 20 to 50. Price is on the vertical axis. What is the slope of the line between these points?

mistakes.why: You divided the run by the rise. Slope is the change in the vertical value over the change in the horizontal value: 6 / 30.

items.q: A line on a graph rises from left to right. What is true of its slope?
options: It is negative
It is positive
It is zero
It is undefined

items.q: On a graph with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, a curve is a vertical line at a quantity of 50. What does it show?
options: The quantity is 50 at every price
The price is 50 at every quantity
Quantity rises as price rises
Quantity falls as price rises

items.q: What is the slope of a horizontal line?
options: One, because it runs straight across the whole graph
Negative, because it runs to the right
It changes from point to point
Zero, because the vertical value does not change

items.q: A straight line and a curve that bows outward both run from the vertical axis down to the horizontal axis. How do their slopes differ?
options: Both have the same slope at every point
The line gets steeper as it moves right; the bowed curve does not
The line's slope is the same at every point; the bowed curve gets steeper as it moves right
The bowed curve has a positive slope and the line a negative slope

items.q: Using the table, what is the slope of the line, with price on the vertical axis?

mistakes.why: You dropped the sign. Price falls as quantity rises, so the slope is negative.
You divided the run by the rise. Slope is the change in price (vertical) over the change in quantity (horizontal).

items.q: How would you describe the curve drawn from the table?
options: Upward sloping: a positive slope from point to point
Downward sloping: a negative slope
A vertical line
A horizontal line

items.q: If the line from the table keeps the same slope, what price goes with a quantity of 50 sandwiches?
Place point X on the upward-sloping curve at a higher price than the marked starting point.
Place point X on the downward-sloping curve at a larger quantity than the marked starting point.
Buyers' incomes rise, and at every price they now want more concert tickets than before. Shift the right curve the right way.

slips.S: Incomes belong to buyers, so they move the demand curve D; sellers' costs would move S.

items.q: A storm destroys a third of the orange groves, so at every price growers can offer fewer oranges. Shift the right curve the right way.

key.because: a storm that destroys orange groves

slips.D: The storm changes what growers can offer, so it moves S, not the buyers' curve D.

items.q: The price of concert tickets rises and nothing else changes. Place point X where buyers end up on the curve D.
On a graph with price on the vertical axis, which change causes a movement along a curve rather than a shift of it?
options: A change in the incomes of the good's buyers
A change in the price of the good itself
A change in the number of sellers
A change in buyers' tastes

items.q: A curve "shifts right". On a graph with quantity on the horizontal axis, what does that mean?
options: At every price, the quantity is larger than before
At every quantity, the price is lower than before
The price rose and the quantity rose along the same curve
The curve became steeper

items.q: Why does an economist say "ceteris paribus" when drawing a curve?
options: To say the curve is a straight line
To say the two variables have a direct relationship
To say the curve will shift soon
To hold everything except the two graphed variables constant

items.q: A student reads a graph and says, "The price fell, so the curve D shifted right." What is wrong with the claim?
options: A fall in price shifts D left, not right
Price is on the horizontal axis, so it does not move D
A change in price moves along D; it does not shift D
Nothing: a lower price shifts D right

items.q: Make the explanation specific: a cafe raises the price of its muffins and sells fewer. Fill in each blank.

specific.frame: The ___ changed, and it is the variable on ___, so the graph shows ___.

variable.label: What changed
options: price of muffins
number of buyers
buyers' tastes

why.1: The scenario changes the muffin price; the number of buyers is not mentioned.
why.2: Nothing in the scenario changes tastes; only the price moves.

because.label: Where it sits
options: the vertical axis
neither axis

why.1: On a market graph price is on the vertical axis.

change.label: What the graph shows
options: a movement along the curve
a shift of the curve

why.1: Only a change in something off the axes shifts the curve; a price change moves along it.

specific.model: The price of muffins rose, and price is the variable on the vertical axis, so the cafe moves along its curve D to a smaller quantity because buyers want fewer muffins at a higher price.

items.q: In week 1 the coffee shop cuts the latte price from $5 to $4. How does its graph show this?
options: A shift of the whole curve D to the right, at each price
A movement down along D to a larger quantity
A shift of D to the left
A movement up along D to a smaller quantity

items.q: In week 2 a large office building opens next door. How does the graph show this?
options: D shifts right: more lattes are wanted at every price
A movement down along the curve D, as after a price cut
D shifts left: fewer lattes are wanted at each price
No change, because the price did not change

items.q: In week 3 a rival cafe gives away free iced tea. What is the most likely change on the coffee shop's graph?
options: D shifts right: customers want more drinks
A movement up along D
A movement down along D
D shifts left: some customers drink free tea instead

items.q: Put the steps for deciding between a shift and a movement in order.
options: Name what changed in the scenario
Check whether it is the variable on one of the axes
If it is, move along the curve; if not, shift the curve
Show the direction with an arrow and label the new curve

items.q: Buyers want more umbrellas at every price after a rainy forecast. Shift the right curve and mark the new point where the curves cross.

key.because: a rainy forecast that makes buyers want more umbrellas

slips.S: The forecast changes what buyers want, so it moves D; sellers' costs have not changed.

items.q: A new machine lets bakers make bread more cheaply, so at every price they offer more loaves. Shift the right curve and mark the new crossing.

key.because: a machine that lowers bakers' costs

slips.D: The machine changes what bakers can offer, so it moves S, not the buyers' curve D.

items.q: On a market graph, what does the point where the two curves cross show?
options: The highest price buyers will pay
The one price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer
The lowest price sellers will accept
The price at which nothing is sold

items.q: Which curve moved in the graph?
options: D shifted left
D shifted right
S shifted left
S shifted right

items.q: Compared with the first crossing, where is the new crossing in the graph?
options: At a higher price and a larger quantity
At a lower price and a larger quantity
At the same price and a smaller quantity
At a lower price and a smaller quantity

items.q: Which event could have caused the change in the graph?
options: Sellers' costs for materials fall
More sellers enter the market
Buyers learn that a cheaper rival product works just as well
Buyers come to expect the price of the product to rise next month

items.q: At which price in the table do the two curves cross?
Using the table, at a price of $10, how many more cases do buyers want than sellers offer each week?

mistakes.why: You added the two quantities. The gap between them is the larger minus the smaller: 80 - 20.
That is the gap at $15 plus another row. Read the $10 row only: 80 wanted, 20 offered.

items.q: Sellers find a cheaper supplier, and at each price they now offer 20 more cases than in the table. At what price do the curves cross now?
To compare two crossings on an exam graph, what should you show?
options: The new crossing by itself, since the old one no longer matters
The curves alone, since the crossings are obvious
The new curve drawn over the old one with no labels
Both crossings, each with dashed lines to both axes, labeled with the old and new price and quantity
